parenting_scripts.title: Bedtime Meltdown
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child is screaming, crying, or having a full tantrum when it's time for bed
prevention_tips: Maintain consistent bedtime routine
Start wind-down activities 30 minutes before bed
Ensure child isn't overtired - watch for early sleep cues
Keep bedroom cool, dark, and comfortable
Avoid stimulating activities close to bedtime

strategies.name: Validation and Boundary
strategies.why_it_works: Acknowledging the child's emotions while maintaining the boundary shows them their feelings are valid, but the expectation remains. Offering choices gives them control within your structure.
script: You're really upset about bedtime. I can see this is hard for you.
AND bedtime is still happening. You need your sleep to feel good tomorrow.
Do you want to walk to your room or should I carry you?
I'm here for you while you have these big feelings.
strategies.mantra: This is temporary. Their big feelings don't mean I'm doing something wrong. Consistency is kindness.

strategies.name: Playful Approach
strategies.why_it_works: Playfulness can shift the emotional state and make cooperation more likely. It maintains the boundary while reducing power struggles through connection.
script: Oh no! Did the bedtime monster get you? It makes kids SO mad about going to bed!
Hey, should we march to bed like soldiers or hop like bunnies?
Your stuffies are probably waiting for you. Want to go say goodnight to them?
Even when you're upset, I love you so much. Come on, let's get you ready for bed.
strategies.mantra: This is temporary. Their big feelings don't mean I'm doing something wrong. Consistency is kindness.

strategies.name: Limited Choices
strategies.why_it_works: Offering choices within the non-negotiable boundary gives children a sense of autonomy and control, making them more likely to cooperate.
script: I know bedtime feels like too much right now.
You can choose: PJs first or brush teeth first?
Want your door open a little or closed tonight?
It's bedtime now, and you get to decide if we do this the easy way or the hard way.
strategies.mantra: This is temporary. Their big feelings don't mean I'm doing something wrong. Consistency is kindness.

parenting_scripts.title: Sibling Toy Fight
parenting_scripts.scenario: Two children are fighting, grabbing, or screaming over the same toy
prevention_tips: Teach taking turns before conflicts arise
Have multiple similar toys available
Create clear expectations about sharing
Set up play environments that reduce competition
Practice problem-solving when everyone is calm

strategies.name: Sportscaster Approach
strategies.why_it_works: Refusing to pick sides prevents you from becoming the referee and teaches kids to work together. Taking the toy away removes the immediate trigger while they regulate.
script: I see two kids who both want the same toy. That's really frustrating!
I'm not choosing who gets it. You both want it - I get that.
The toy's taking a break until you can work this out together.
When you're ready to figure this out, I'll help you think of ideas.
strategies.mantra: I don't need to solve this FOR them. I can help them solve it together.

strategies.name: Empathy for Both
strategies.why_it_works: Validating both children's perspectives helps them feel heard and reduces the intensity of the conflict. Giving them time to think promotes problem-solving skills.
script: Sarah, you're upset because you want the doll. Jake, you're upset because you had it first.
Both of your feelings make total sense to me.
Here's what's going to happen: I'm going to set a timer for 2 minutes. You can each think of ideas.
Then we'll come back together and you can share your solutions.
strategies.mantra: I don't need to solve this FOR them. I can help them solve it together.

strategies.name: Immediate Safety
strategies.why_it_works: Physical separation prevents escalation and gives both children space to regulate their emotions before attempting problem-solving.
script: I see grabbing hands and loud voices. I need to keep everyone safe.
Sarah, come with me to the kitchen. Jake, you stay here please.
When you're both calm, we'll talk about the toy.
Right now I'm making sure everyone's safe.
strategies.mantra: I don't need to solve this FOR them. I can help them solve it together.

parenting_scripts.title: School Morning Refusal
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child is refusing to get dressed, hiding, or melting down about going to school
prevention_tips: Prepare clothes and backpack the night before
Ensure adequate sleep (early bedtime)
Build in extra time for morning routine
Address any school anxieties during calm moments
Create visual morning routine charts

strategies.name: Acknowledge and Action
strategies.why_it_works: Validating their feelings while moving forward with the plan shows them you can handle their big emotions and still keep them safe with routines.
script: I can tell something about school feels hard today.
AND school is still happening. Let's get you ready.
You can get dressed yourself, or I can help. What do you want?
We're leaving in 5 minutes. You've got this.
strategies.mantra: Their resistance doesn't mean I should give in. Structure feels safe even when they fight it.

strategies.name: Connect First
strategies.why_it_works: Connection before direction helps children feel understood and supported, making them more willing to cooperate with necessary tasks.
script: Come here, sweetheart. This morning feels really hard, doesn't it?
Tell me what's going on with school today.
That sounds really [hard/scary/frustrating]. I totally get it.
Even when school feels tough, I know you can do it. Let's get ready together.
strategies.mantra: Their resistance doesn't mean I should give in. Structure feels safe even when they fight it.

strategies.name: Playful Power
strategies.why_it_works: Playfulness can transform resistance into cooperation by making necessary tasks feel like games rather than demands.
script: Oh no! Your clothes are playing hide and seek!
Let's catch that sneaky shirt! I think it's hiding behind the door!
I wonder if your backpack's ready for today's adventure...
You're going to school today, and I'll be right here when you get home.
strategies.mantra: Their resistance doesn't mean I should give in. Structure feels safe even when they fight it.

parenting_scripts.title: "I Hate You!" Outburst
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child screams "I hate you!" or "You're not my friend!" during a conflict
prevention_tips: Model emotional regulation during your own frustrations
Teach feeling words when child is calm
Validate emotions regularly before they escalate
Create safe spaces for expressing difficult feelings
Maintain strong connection through daily one-on-one time

strategies.name: Stay Calm and Reflect
strategies.why_it_works: Staying calm in the face of hurtful words models emotional regulation and shows them their big feelings can't push you away or change your boundaries.
script: You're really mad at me right now. You wish I'd change my mind.
It's totally okay to be angry with me. I can handle it.
Even when you're mad, I love you so much.
When you're ready, I'm here for you. My answer is still [boundary].
strategies.mantra: They don't actually hate me. This is their immature brain trying to get control. I can stay steady.

strategies.name: Name the Feeling
strategies.why_it_works: Naming emotions helps children understand what they're feeling and teaches them that all feelings are acceptable, even when expressed imperfectly.
script: Wow, those are some really big angry feelings coming out.
You're so frustrated you're using your strongest words to tell me.
I hear you. You wish things were different.
I love you even when you're angry. Even with those words.
strategies.mantra: They don't actually hate me. This is their immature brain trying to get control. I can stay steady.

strategies.name: Empathy Bridge
strategies.why_it_works: Sharing your own experience with similar feelings helps children feel less alone and shows them that strong emotions are normal and manageable.
script: You know what? Sometimes I get really frustrated with people I love too.
When you say you hate me, I think you mean you hate what I'm asking.
I totally get it. This rule feels super unfair right now.
And I still love you tons. And the rule still stands.
strategies.mantra: They don't actually hate me. This is their immature brain trying to get control. I can stay steady.

parenting_scripts.title: Doctor Visit Anxiety
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child is crying, clinging, or refusing to cooperate at a medical appointment
prevention_tips: Read books about doctor visits beforehand
Role-play doctor appointments with toys
Bring comfort items (favorite stuffed animal)
Schedule appointments when child is well-rested
Prepare child with age-appropriate explanations

strategies.name: Validation and Partnership
strategies.why_it_works: Providing information reduces anxiety by making the unknown known. Staying physically close activates their attachment system and helps them feel safe.
script: You're scared about being here. Doctor visits can feel really big.
I'll stay right next to you the whole time.
We're a team. You don't have to be brave by yourself.
After this, we'll [specific plan]. That'll be nice.
strategies.mantra: Their fear is real and valid. I can be their calm in this storm.

strategies.name: Control and Information
strategies.why_it_works: Detailed information helps reduce anxiety by eliminating unknowns. Offering choices gives them some control in a situation where they feel powerless.
script: Let me tell you exactly what's going to happen so your brain can get ready.
First [step 1], then [step 2]. I'll be holding your hand.
You get to choose: do you want to sit on my lap or on the table?
If you need to cry or squeeze my hand, that's totally okay.
strategies.mantra: Their fear is real and valid. I can be their calm in this storm.

strategies.name: Coping Tools
strategies.why_it_works: Teaching specific coping strategies gives children tools they can use to manage anxiety in this and future situations.
script: Let's take three deep breaths together. In through your nose, out through your mouth.
I want you to look at me and think about [favorite comfort item/memory].
You can hold my hand as tight as you need to.
This will be over soon, and then we'll [comfort activity].
strategies.mantra: Their fear is real and valid. I can be their calm in this storm.

parenting_scripts.title: Transition Defiance
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child refuses to stop current activity for transition (leaving park, turning off TV, ending playtime)
prevention_tips: Give 10-minute and 5-minute warnings before transitions
Use visual timers that children can see
Create predictable daily routines
Acknowledge how fun the current activity is
Plan appealing next activities to look forward to

strategies.name: Time and Choice
strategies.why_it_works: Acknowledging their disappointment while maintaining the boundary teaches them that feelings are valid but don't control actions. Advance notice helps their brain prepare.
script: I see you don't want to stop. This is really fun for you.
We have 2 more minutes. Use them however you want.
When the timer beeps, we're going. You can walk or I can carry you.
It's hard when fun things end. We still need to go.
strategies.mantra: Transitions are hard for kids. Staying consistent helps them trust the structure.

strategies.name: Emotional Validation
strategies.why_it_works: Validating disappointment helps children feel understood while learning that they can have feelings and still follow through with necessary actions.
script: You wish you could play forever. That makes total sense to me.
It's disappointing when fun things have to end.
You can be sad about leaving AND we're still leaving now.
I'll remember how much you loved this for next time.
strategies.mantra: Transitions are hard for kids. Staying consistent helps them trust the structure.

strategies.name: Future Focus
strategies.why_it_works: Focusing on what comes next helps shift their attention from what they're losing to what they're gaining, making transitions easier.
script: I know it's hard to leave. Let's talk about what we're going to do next.
After we leave here, we're going to [next activity].
And tomorrow/later we can [plan for return/similar activity].
Right now your body needs to come with me, even if your feelings aren't ready.
strategies.mantra: Transitions are hard for kids. Staying consistent helps them trust the structure.

parenting_scripts.title: Physical Aggression
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child hits, bites, kicks, or throws things when upset
prevention_tips: Teach physical outlets for big emotions before they're needed
Identify triggers that lead to aggressive behavior
Ensure child gets enough physical activity daily
Model calm conflict resolution in your own interactions
Address underlying needs (hunger, tiredness, overstimulation)

strategies.name: Immediate Safety
strategies.why_it_works: Stopping the behavior immediately while validating the emotion teaches them that all feelings are okay, but not all actions are okay. Offering alternatives gives them appropriate outlets.
script: I won't let you hit. I need to keep everyone safe.
I'm moving you/myself so no one gets hurt.
You have big feelings AND hitting's not okay.
When you're calm, we can talk about what happened.
strategies.mantra: This behavior is communication, not manipulation. They need my help learning better ways to express themselves.

strategies.name: Feeling and Boundary
strategies.why_it_works: Separating feelings from actions helps children understand that emotions are always acceptable, but behaviors have limits and consequences.
script: You're so angry you want to hit. I get it.
AND I won't let you hurt me or anyone else.
Being angry is okay. Hitting is not.
Let's find a safe way to get those big feelings out.
strategies.mantra: This behavior is communication, not manipulation. They need my help learning better ways to express themselves.

strategies.name: Redirect Energy
strategies.why_it_works: Providing physical outlets for big emotions helps children learn appropriate ways to release intense feelings while keeping everyone safe.
script: I see you've got lots of big energy that needs to come out.
You can punch this pillow, stomp hard, or squeeze your fists super tight.
Your feelings matter AND everyone needs to stay safe.
I'll help you find a good way to let those feelings out.
strategies.mantra: This behavior is communication, not manipulation. They need my help learning better ways to express themselves.

parenting_scripts.title: Grocery Store Meltdown
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child has a tantrum in public, attracting stares and making shopping impossible
prevention_tips: Shop when child is well-rested and fed
Bring snacks and small activities/toys
Set clear expectations before entering the store
Keep shopping trips short for younger children
Consider online grocery pickup for challenging periods

strategies.name: Strategic Exit
strategies.why_it_works: Removing overwhelming stimuli helps children regulate. Public spaces can be overstimulating, and a change of environment often helps reset their nervous system.
script: I can see this is really overwhelming for you right now.
We're going to take a break outside where it's quieter.
You can have your feelings, and we need to keep everyone safe.
When you're ready, we can decide together if we continue shopping or come back later.
strategies.mantra: Other people's opinions don't matter. My child needs my calm presence right now.

strategies.name: Stay and Support
strategies.why_it_works: Staying present shows the child they're not alone in their big emotions. It models that feelings are manageable and temporary.
script: You're having such big feelings right now. I'm right here with you.
I can see you really wanted [item]. It's disappointing when we can't have what we want.
I'm going to stay close while you have these feelings.
When you're ready, we can finish our shopping together.
strategies.mantra: This is temporary. I'm teaching them they're safe to have big emotions with me.

strategies.name: Distraction and Redirect
strategies.why_it_works: Redirecting to a helpful task can shift focus from the upset to feeling useful and important, while validating their emotions.
script: Wow, look how upset your body is! That's some really big energy.
I wonder... can you help me find the red apples? I need someone with good eyes.
You're still upset AND you can help me with this important job.
Thank you for helping me even when your feelings are big.
strategies.mantra: Sometimes giving them a job helps them feel important and shifts their focus.

parenting_scripts.title: Car Seat Refusal
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child refuses to get in car seat, arches back, or fights the safety straps
prevention_tips: Ensure car seat is properly adjusted and comfortable
Bring special car toys or music only for car rides
Practice buckling with stuffed animals at home
Allow extra time so you don't feel rushed
Address any discomfort issues (temperature, straps, etc.)

strategies.name: Safety First
strategies.why_it_works: Clear boundaries around safety while acknowledging their feelings shows them that some things are non-negotiable, but you still care about their emotions.
script: Your body is saying no to the car seat. I hear that.
AND my job is to keep you safe. Car seats keep bodies safe in cars.
I'm going to help you get buckled in. You can be upset while I do my job.
As soon as you're safe, we can talk about what's making this hard.
strategies.mantra: Safety is not negotiable. I can be firm AND loving.

strategies.name: Choice Within Safety
strategies.why_it_works: Offering choices within the safety requirement gives them some control while maintaining the boundary. It helps them feel less powerless.
script: The car seat is happening because I need to keep you safe.
You get to choose: Would you like to climb in yourself or would you like me to help you?
Would you like to hold [comfort item] or choose our driving music?
Your body goes in the seat, and you can choose how to make it more comfortable.
strategies.mantra: I can give choices within the non-negotiable boundary.

strategies.name: Connection First
strategies.why_it_works: Taking time to understand their resistance often reveals specific concerns (discomfort, wanting independence) that can be addressed while maintaining safety.
script: Come here first. I can see you really don't want to get in your seat.
Tell me what's hard about the car seat today.
That makes sense. [Validate their concern].
I still need to keep you safe, and now I understand better how you're feeling.
strategies.mantra: Understanding their perspective doesn't mean changing the boundary.

parenting_scripts.title: Homework Battles
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child melts down, refuses to start, or has emotional outbursts about homework
prevention_tips: Establish consistent homework time and space
Ensure child has had snack and movement before starting
Break large assignments into smaller chunks
Communicate with teachers about appropriate homework load
Create a calm, organized workspace free from distractions

strategies.name: Break It Down
strategies.why_it_works: Overwhelming tasks trigger the fight-or-flight response. Breaking work into smaller chunks makes it feel achievable and reduces anxiety.
script: This homework feels really big and overwhelming to your brain right now.
Let's look at it together and break it into tiny pieces.
You don't have to do ALL of it right now. Just one small part.
I believe your brain can handle this when we make it smaller.
strategies.mantra: Big tasks feel impossible to kids. I can help them see it's manageable.

strategies.name: Emotional First Aid
strategies.why_it_works: When children are in emotional distress, their prefrontal cortex (learning brain) goes offline. Emotional regulation must come before academic work.
script: Your body is telling me this feels really hard right now.
Let's take care of your big feelings first, then we'll tackle the homework.
Sometimes our brains need a break before they can learn new things.
When you're feeling calmer, your brain will be ready to work.
strategies.mantra: Learning can't happen when they're emotionally flooded. Feelings first, then academics.

strategies.name: Partnership Approach
strategies.why_it_works: Taking over homework robs children of the opportunity to build resilience and problem-solving skills. Support without rescue builds confidence.
script: This homework is your job, and I'm here to support you.
What part feels hardest to you? Let's start with something easier.
I'm not going to do it for you, but I'll sit nearby while you work.
You're capable of figuring this out. I'm here if you need help.
strategies.mantra: I'm their coach, not their replacement. They need to build confidence in their own abilities.

parenting_scripts.title: Morning Routine Chaos
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child is slow, distracted, or melting down during morning routine
prevention_tips: Prepare everything possible the night before
Wake up 15 minutes earlier to reduce time pressure
Create visual morning routine charts
Ensure child gets adequate sleep (adjust bedtime if needed)
Build in buffer time for unexpected delays

strategies.name: Calm Urgency
strategies.why_it_works: Modeling calm urgency instead of frantic rushing helps children focus better and reduces morning stress for everyone.
script: I can see you're moving slowly this morning. Sometimes our bodies feel sluggish.
We need to leave in 10 minutes. That's enough time if we focus.
What's the most important thing you need to do right now?
I'm going to help you stay on track without rushing your body.
strategies.mantra: I can be calm AND keep us moving. Panic makes everything harder.

strategies.name: Choice Sequence
strategies.why_it_works: Children resist being controlled but respond well to having choices. Sequencing gives them autonomy within the necessary tasks.
script: You have three things left: getting dressed, eating breakfast, and brushing teeth.
Which one do you want to do first?
Great choice. After that, you can pick what comes next.
You're in charge of the order, and all three need to happen before we leave.
strategies.mantra: Giving them control over the sequence helps them feel empowered while everything still gets done.

strategies.name: Reset and Reconnect
strategies.why_it_works: When mornings go badly, taking a moment to reconnect can shift the entire dynamic and actually save time by reducing resistance.
script: This morning feels hard for both of us. Let's take a quick reset.
Give me a hug. We're going to figure this out together.
What would help your body feel more ready for the day?
We have a few minutes to make this morning feel better before we go.
strategies.mantra: Connection is more important than being on time. A good relationship with my child matters most.

parenting_scripts.title: Screen Time Battles
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child refuses to turn off devices, has meltdowns when screen time ends
prevention_tips: Set clear screen time limits before starting
Use visual timers that count down
Plan appealing activities to transition to
Create screen-free times (meals, bedtime routine)
Model healthy screen use yourself

strategies.name: Advance Warning
strategies.why_it_works: Sudden transitions from preferred activities trigger big emotions. Advance warning allows the brain time to mentally prepare for the change.
script: You have 5 more minutes of screen time, then it's time to turn it off.
I know it's hard to stop when you're having fun. Let's set a timer together.
When the timer goes off, screen time is done. What do you want to do next?
I'll help you turn it off when the timer rings.
strategies.mantra: Transitions are hard for kids. Advance notice helps their brain prepare for the change.

strategies.name: Validate and Redirect
strategies.why_it_works: Validating their disappointment while offering appealing alternatives helps shift their focus from what they're losing to what they're gaining.
script: You're so disappointed that screen time is over. That makes total sense.
It's hard when fun things have to end. You wish you could keep playing.
The screen is going away now, AND we can find something else fun to do.
What sounds interesting: building with blocks, going outside, or reading together?
strategies.mantra: Their disappointment is valid. I can acknowledge it while still maintaining the boundary.

strategies.name: Collaborative Solution
strategies.why_it_works: When children participate in creating solutions, they feel ownership and are more likely to cooperate. It builds problem-solving skills too.
script: Screen time battles are hard for both of us. Let's solve this together.
What would help you remember when screen time is almost over?
How can we make turning off screens feel less terrible?
Let's come up with a plan that works for both of us.
strategies.mantra: Kids are more likely to follow rules they help create. Including them in problem-solving builds cooperation.

parenting_scripts.title: Potty Training Refusal
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child refuses to try the potty, wants to stay in diapers, or resists potty learning
prevention_tips: Wait for genuine readiness signs before starting
Make potty visible and accessible without pressure
Read potty books together casually
Let child observe family members using toilet
Avoid comparing to other children or setting arbitrary timelines

strategies.name: Follow Their Lead
strategies.why_it_works: Potty learning is about body sovereignty. Pressure creates power struggles and delays success. When children feel in control of their own body, they're more motivated to learn.
script: Your body is yours. You're in charge of when you're ready for the potty.
Some kids use the potty, some kids use diapers. When you're ready, you can decide.
I'm not going to make you try. This is your choice about your body.
I believe you'll figure this out when your body is ready.
strategies.mantra: My child will figure this out. Pressure doesn't help learning, it creates resistance.

strategies.name: Curiosity Without Pressure
strategies.why_it_works: Normalizing the potty through exploration removes fear and builds familiarity. When it's just another interesting object, children are more likely to try it.
script: Want to check out the potty with me? No using it, just looking.
Your teddy might want to try sitting on the potty. Let's help them.
I'm going to use the bathroom. Want to come see how it works?
The potty is here whenever you feel curious about it.
strategies.mantra: Familiarity reduces resistance. I can create curiosity without creating pressure.

strategies.name: Acknowledge Their Feelings
strategies.why_it_works: Resistance often masks fear or anxiety. Acknowledging feelings helps children feel understood and reduces the emotional charge around potty learning.
script: You seem worried about the potty. What feels hard about it?
Trying new things can feel scary. That makes sense.
You like diapers because you already know them. I get that.
When you're ready to talk about the potty, I'm here to listen.
strategies.mantra: Their resistance is communication, not defiance. I can stay curious about what they need.

parenting_scripts.title: Potty Training Accidents
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child has potty accident and is upset, embarrassed, or showing shame
prevention_tips: Normalize that accidents are part of learning
Keep spare clothes easily accessible everywhere
Avoid over-praising potty success (reduces shame around accidents)
Watch for early signals and offer gentle reminders
Ensure child is actually developmentally ready for potty learning

strategies.name: Matter-of-Fact Response
strategies.why_it_works: Staying neutral prevents shame from forming. Accidents are data points, not failures. Your calm reaction teaches them that mistakes are safe and normal.
script: Your pants are wet. Let's get you dry clothes.
Pee came out. That happens when bodies are learning.
No big deal. Let's clean this up together.
Bodies are figuring out what that feeling means before pee comes. You're learning.
strategies.mantra: Accidents are not failures. They're learning opportunities. My calm matters more than the mess.

strategies.name: No-Shame Language
strategies.why_it_works: Shame interferes with learning and damages the parent-child relationship. De-shaming language keeps their self-worth intact while they master this skill.
script: You're still learning. This is what learning looks like.
Next time you'll catch that feeling a little sooner.
Your body is getting better at recognizing that feeling.
Everyone has accidents when they're learning something new.
strategies.mantra: Shame doesn't teach. It only makes learning harder and damages their confidence.

strategies.name: Problem-Solving Together
strategies.why_it_works: Involving children in solutions helps them feel capable and builds problem-solving skills. It shifts from failure to learning opportunity.
script: You had an accident. What do you think we should do?
Can you help me figure out how to clean this up?
What was happening before the pee came? Let's be detectives.
Next time you feel that feeling, what could you do differently?
strategies.mantra: I can help them learn from this without making them feel bad about themselves.

parenting_scripts.title: Poop Withholding Anxiety
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child is afraid to poop on potty, holds poop for days, or shows anxiety about pooping
prevention_tips: Separate pee and poop learning (pee first, poop later)
Teach about body continuity (poop is extra, not a body part)
Avoid showing disgust or negative reactions to poop
Ensure diet supports easy bowel movements
Model casual, positive attitudes about pooping yourself

strategies.name: Body Continuity Education
strategies.why_it_works: Young children worry about body parts separating. Understanding that poop is 'extra food' not a body part reduces existential anxiety about pooping.
script: Your body is so smart! It takes what it needs from food and gets rid of extra.
Poop is the extra stuff your body doesn't need. Your body stays whole and safe.
It's kind of like a snack - your body keeps the part it needs, and lets the rest go as poop.
After poop comes out, we say bye to it! It's done its job helping your body.
strategies.mantra: This anxiety is developmental and normal. Education reduces fear more than pressure ever could.

strategies.name: Gradual Desensitization
strategies.why_it_works: Forcing creates trauma. Gradual exposure lets them build comfort at their own pace. Each small step builds confidence for the next.
script: You can poop in your diaper in your room. No rush.
Want to try pooping in your diaper while in the bathroom? Just to get comfortable.
How about sitting on the potty with your diaper on? Just practicing.
You're getting closer. Your body is figuring this out at your speed.
strategies.mantra: Slow is fast. Forcing creates trauma. Gradual steps build lasting success.

strategies.name: Manage Your Own Anxiety
strategies.why_it_works: Children absorb parental anxiety. Your belief in their capability becomes their belief. Your calm is contagious.
script: I notice I'm worried about this, and that's my feeling, not your problem.
My child's struggles today don't predict struggles months from now.
I can be patient while their body figures this out.
This is temporary. They will not be withholding poop when they're 10.
strategies.mantra: Yes, they're struggling, AND yes, they will figure this out. My confidence helps theirs grow.

parenting_scripts.title: Losing at Games Meltdown
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child screams, throws pieces, or refuses to keep playing after losing a game
prevention_tips: Talk about winning and losing during calm moments, not mid-game
Before playing, ask what could help if the game starts to feel frustrating
Choose some games based on chance so losing isn't about being "not good enough"
Praise effort and persistence more than the final score
Normalize disappointment as something everyone feels, including you
Model losing gracefully yourself during family game nights

strategies.name: Name the Feeling First
strategies.why_it_works: Naming the disappointment out loud helps a flooded child feel understood instead of corrected, which lowers the intensity faster than logic or a lecture about sportsmanship. It also hands them the words to use next time, which is the real skill being built.
script: You really wanted to win that game. Losing it feels terrible right now.
I can see you're angry and disappointed. Those are big feelings.
It's okay to feel upset about losing. It's not okay to throw the pieces.
I'm going to keep these safe for a second. I'm right here with you.
strategies.mantra: Losing hurts them right now. That's not bad sportsmanship, it's how much they cared.

strategies.name: Pause Before Teaching
strategies.why_it_works: A dysregulated child can't absorb a lesson about gracious losing yet because the thinking part of their brain is offline. Giving space and waiting for the storm to pass means any conversation afterward actually lands instead of bouncing off.
script: You don't have to talk right now. I'll sit close by.
Take whatever time you need to feel better.
I'm not upset with you. I'm just going to wait here.
When you're ready, we can talk about what happened.
strategies.mantra: Losing hurts them right now. That's not bad sportsmanship, it's how much they cared.

strategies.name: Rematch and Reframe
strategies.why_it_works: Framing losing as one round in an ongoing relationship, rather than a verdict, builds resilience faster than being told to just get over it. Offering a real rematch turns the lesson into practice instead of a talk.
script: Sometimes we win, sometimes we lose. That's how games work, for everyone.
Losing today doesn't mean losing always. Want to play again?
Try telling me "I'm really disappointed I didn't win" instead of throwing.
I'm proud of you for staying at the table, even when it was hard.
strategies.mantra: Losing hurts them right now. That's not bad sportsmanship, it's how much they cared.

parenting_scripts.title: Drop-off Separation Panic
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child sobs, clings, and refuses to let go at the classroom door during drop-off
prevention_tips: Put the morning routine on the wall as pictures, not spoken minutes
Rehearse the goodbye in play with toys before the first day
Build a countdown they can touch and move themselves
Keep the goodbye short and identical every single day
Tuck a comfort object or small photo of you into their bag
Ask the teacher how long the crying actually lasts once you leave

strategies.name: Short, Certain Goodbye
strategies.why_it_works: A child's body reads a parent leaving as danger even when they know the room is safe, and a drawn-out or repeated goodbye confirms that doubt instead of settling it. A brief, identical goodbye followed by actually leaving is what teaches their body this is safe.
script: Big squeeze, our two words, and I'll see you after snack.
I know you want me to stay. I can't, and you are going to be okay.
Ms. Bianchi is right here with you. You can do hard things.
I'll see you soon. I always come back.
strategies.mantra: My calm is the message. Some kids just need longer, not a new plan.

strategies.name: Validate, Then Go
strategies.why_it_works: Naming the resistance as a real feeling instead of arguing with it lowers the temperature without inviting a debate you can't win at the door. Pairing validation with a held boundary teaches that both can be true, they can be upset and it can still be a school day.
script: You really don't want me to go today. That's allowed.
It's still a school day. My job is to keep you safe, and today that means you stay and play.
You can be sad about goodbye. I'll still be back at pickup.
I love you. I'll see you very soon.
strategies.mantra: My calm is the message. Some kids just need longer, not a new plan.

strategies.name: Countdown and Rehearsal
strategies.why_it_works: Making the unknown familiar ahead of time, with a practiced goodbye and a visible countdown, shrinks the panic before it starts because the moment stops being a surprise. Rehearsing on a stuffed animal lets a child try the hard part out in a low-stakes way first.
script: See these beads? One comes off each morning until it's a school day.
Let's practice our goodbye on Rabbit first, big squeeze, two words, all done.
Your teacher's name is Ms. Bianchi. I heard she keeps dinosaur books in her reading corner.
We're going to do the exact same goodbye every day, so it stops feeling scary.
strategies.mantra: My calm is the message. Some kids just need longer, not a new plan.

parenting_scripts.title: Gift Disappointment in Public
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child opens a gift in front of family, visibly deflates, and says out loud they wanted something else
prevention_tips: Talk with your child ahead of big gift occasions about how disappointment can feel
Never squeeze out a "thank you" while the room is still watching
Practice gracious reactions in low-stakes moments, like games at home
Model handling your own small letdowns calmly in front of your child
Have a private phrase ready that means "let's step away for a second"
Save the manners conversation for later, never mid-table

strategies.name: Feeling Before Manners
strategies.why_it_works: A letdown that gets acknowledged starts to shrink, while one that gets corrected in front of an audience digs in and piles shame on top. Going for the feeling first, and buying a quiet exit if the room is too hot, gets you both through the moment without a scene.
script: Not the one you were hoping for. I saw that land.
That's allowed. You can feel disappointed for a second.
Let's get some water. Come with me for a minute.
We don't have to figure out what to say to Aunt Mara right this second.
strategies.mantra: The hot face in the room is mine. Handle their feeling first, my embarrassment can wait.

strategies.name: Both Feelings Can Be True
strategies.why_it_works: Being let down about a gift doesn't erase noticing that someone made an effort, and the two feelings can sit side by side instead of fighting each other. Letting them coexist, without demanding one replace the other, teaches real emotional honesty instead of a performed one.
script: You wanted the other kind. I know that's true.
And Grandma drove a long way to pick something just for you. That's also true.
You can feel both of those at the same time. They don't cancel each other out.
You don't have to pretend you love it right now.
strategies.mantra: The hot face in the room is mine. Handle their feeling first, my embarrassment can wait.

strategies.name: Repair Later, Privately
strategies.why_it_works: Doing the repair once everyone is calm, instead of squeezing out a performance in the moment, is what actually grows genuine gratitude over time. A specific, true thing to say works better than a generic forced thank-you because it's something the child actually means.
script: Earlier was a hard moment, and you handled the big feeling well.
What's one true thing we could tell Aunt Mara about her gift?
You don't have to say you loved it. You can say something real instead.
I'm proud of you for working through that.
strategies.mantra: The hot face in the room is mine. Handle their feeling first, my embarrassment can wait.

parenting_scripts.title: "I Want Papa, Not You!" Moment
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child suddenly rejects one parent, screaming "I want Papa, not you!" right in front of both of you
prevention_tips: Expect preference phases to come and go; they are not a verdict on either parent
Talk with your co-parent about the toll before resentment builds
Keep showing up warmly without demanding to be chosen
Let the preferred parent set their own limits too, needing a break is allowed
Rotate who does bedtime, bath, and drop-off so roles don't calcify
Remember it usually spikes during stress, tiredness, or big transitions

strategies.name: Stay Warm, Don't Take the Bait
strategies.why_it_works: A young child unleashing this on one parent is usually felt-safety collapsing onto a single person during a stressful stretch, not a ranking of who parents better. Staying available without pulling back hurt is what actually shortens the phase.
script: I hear you want Papa right now. That's okay.
I'm still here, and I still love you just the same.
Papa's going to help you with this one. I'll see you in a few minutes.
You don't have to want me back right now. I still want you.
strategies.mantra: They only fall apart this freely with people they trust. It isn't about me, it's a phase with a favorite.

strategies.name: The Preferred Parent Sets a Limit
strategies.why_it_works: Being the chosen parent doesn't mean being available every second, and a child can protest a short break and still come through it fine. Naming the limit calmly, without guilt, models that needs on both sides matter.
script: I hear you want me. I'm going to take a five-minute shower first.
Mama's got you while I'm gone, and I always come back.
You can be upset about waiting. The waiting is still happening.
Thank you for waiting. I'm all yours now.
strategies.mantra: They only fall apart this freely with people they trust. It isn't about me, it's a phase with a favorite.

strategies.name: Team Talk, Away From the Moment
strategies.why_it_works: Processing the toll together, as co-parents, before resentment sets in keeps the rejected parent from quietly withdrawing, which is the one move that tends to prolong the phase. A short debrief turns a hurt feeling into a shared plan instead of a private wound.
script: That was a hard one for me today. Can we talk for a minute?
I know it's not personal, and it still stings sometimes.
Should we swap who does bedtime this week, just to keep it balanced?
I've got bedtime covered tomorrow if it happens again.
strategies.mantra: They only fall apart this freely with people they trust. It isn't about me, it's a phase with a favorite.

parenting_scripts.title: Night Fears of Monsters
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child insists a monster is in the room or under the bed and refuses to settle at bedtime
prevention_tips: Keep a consistent, calming wind-down routine before lights-out
Avoid scary shows, stories, or images close to bedtime
Let a nightlight or an ajar door stay on if it genuinely helps
Talk about fears during the day, not just when they surface at night
Give them a "job," like a flashlight or a stuffed guard, to feel some control
Practice a brief "I can't see you but I can hear you" game during calm daytime moments

strategies.name: Validate the Fear
strategies.why_it_works: Fear is a normal, protective emotion, and dismissing it with "there's nothing there" tends to make a child argue harder or hide the fear instead of managing it. Naming it as real and normal, without reasoning it away, is what actually helps their body settle.
script: You're feeling really scared that something is in your room.
Fear is one of the feelings that helps keep us safe. Everyone feels scared sometimes.
I believe that it feels very real to you right now.
I'm right here, and I'm not going anywhere.
strategies.mantra: I can't take their fear away, but I can help them learn what helps them when it shows up.

strategies.name: Check Together and Reassure
strategies.why_it_works: Walking through the room together turns an abstract dread into something concrete and checkable, which is easier for a young child's brain to file away as safe. Doing the check with them, instead of for them, also hands them a tool to use on their own later.
script: Let's look together. You point to where it feels scary.
See? Just your books and your chair. Nothing else is in here.
Your room is the same safe room it always is.
I'll leave the door open a little so you can hear me nearby.
strategies.mantra: I can't take their fear away, but I can help them learn what helps them when it shows up.

strategies.name: Build a Coping Tool
strategies.why_it_works: Children build real resilience when they get an active role in managing a fear, rather than depending entirely on a parent's reassurance to feel safe. A tangible tool, like a spray bottle or a guard toy, gives them something to do with the fear instead of just feeling it.
script: Let's make monster spray together, water in this bottle, just for the doorway.
Your job is to spray the door before bed. You're in charge of keeping it safe.
Your teddy is on guard duty tonight too. He's a good helper.
Tomorrow you can tell me how your spray worked.
strategies.mantra: I can't take their fear away, but I can help them learn what helps them when it shows up.

parenting_scripts.title: New Sibling Jealousy Outburst
parenting_scripts.scenario: Older child suddenly lashes out at or tries to push away the new baby in a jealous outburst
prevention_tips: Connect with your older child first at every reunion, before turning to the baby
Say out loud that your love for them stays whole, nobody can take their share
Protect short, predictable one-on-one time with just the older child
Give specific, doable ways to be involved instead of vague warnings
Let mixed feelings exist without demanding enthusiasm about the baby
Expect some regression and meet it with calm, not comparison

strategies.name: Block Calmly and Name the Wish
strategies.why_it_works: Stepping in calmly to keep the baby safe, without shaming the older child, addresses the safety issue and the feeling underneath it in the same moment. Naming the wish behind the outburst turns "the baby is a threat" into something you can work with together.
script: I won't let you push him. I'm right here.
You want things to go back to how they were before. That makes sense.
It's hard sharing me right now. That feeling is allowed here.
You can tell me "I don't like this" with words instead.
strategies.mantra: This is a normal response to a big disruption, not a warning sign. Met with calm, it passes sooner.

strategies.name: Love Isn't Something That Runs Out
strategies.why_it_works: Young children quietly assume love works like a fixed amount that gets divided between siblings, and that belief, not wickedness, drives a lot of this behavior. Saying plainly that your love for them stays whole addresses the actual fear underneath the outburst.
script: This baby is lucky, they get you as a big sibling.
My love for you stays all yours. Nobody can take your share.
Some kids feel excited about a baby, some feel grumpy, and lots feel both. All of that is allowed.
I see you. You still matter just as much as you always did.
strategies.mantra: This is a normal response to a big disruption, not a warning sign. Met with calm, it passes sooner.

strategies.name: Protect the One-on-One Time
strategies.why_it_works: Reliable, exclusive time answers the scarcity fear directly instead of just talking about it, since a child who trusts that their turn is coming has less reason to compete with the baby for attention. Naming it as an institution makes the promise feel solid.
script: I'm settling the baby into her nap, and I see you waiting for me. Two more minutes, then I'm all yours.
Saturday morning is ours, just you and me. That's not going to change.
You can stroke her arm gently with one finger, like this, if you want to be near her.
Want to play baby for five minutes? Sometimes being the little one looks cozy.
strategies.mantra: This is a normal response to a big disruption, not a warning sign. Met with calm, it passes sooner.

parenting_scripts.title: Caught in a Lie, Red-Handed
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child flatly denies doing something despite clear evidence right in front of them
prevention_tips: Respond to honesty warmly so telling the truth stays safe, not scary
Avoid interrogating or setting traps to "catch" the lie
Notice patterns in when lying happens, like stress, transitions, or fear of trouble
Model owning your own small mistakes out loud
Keep consequences focused on repair, not shame
Reassure regularly that mistakes are normal and always safe to admit

strategies.name: State the Facts, Skip the Trap
strategies.why_it_works: Naming what you actually see, instead of quizzing them to force a confession, lowers the pressure that makes lying feel necessary in the first place. A calm, factual opening keeps the moment from turning into a standoff neither of you can win.
script: I see the vase is broken, and you told me the dog did it.
I'm not trying to get you in trouble. I want to understand what happened.
It's okay to make mistakes. Everyone breaks things sometimes.
I'd rather hear what really happened than a made-up story.
strategies.mantra: This is emotional communication, not a character flaw. My job is to make the truth feel safe.

strategies.name: Name the Worry Underneath
strategies.why_it_works: Lying at this age is often a child's best attempt to avoid disappointing you or dodge a feared consequence, not deliberate deception. Naming that worry out loud shows them you understand the feeling, which makes the truth easier to hand over.
script: I think you're worried about what will happen if you tell me the truth.
You really didn't want to get in trouble. That makes sense.
It's always safe to tell me, even when it's hard.
Thank you for telling me. That took courage.
strategies.mantra: This is emotional communication, not a character flaw. My job is to make the truth feel safe.

strategies.name: Repair It Together
strategies.why_it_works: Fixing the actual problem together, instead of dispensing a punishment, teaches that honesty leads somewhere useful rather than somewhere painful. When repair is the response, telling the truth stops being the riskier choice.
script: Breaks happen. Let's clean this up together, as a team.
Next time something like this happens, you can just tell me. I promise I'll stay calm.
Try telling me "I'm worried you'll be upset" instead of making up a story.
I love you no matter what. We can always figure out a problem together.
strategies.mantra: This is emotional communication, not a character flaw. My job is to make the truth feel safe.

parenting_scripts.title: The Whining Spiral
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child's whining escalates and repeats even after you've already answered, explained, or given what they asked for
prevention_tips: Notice patterns - whining often clusters around tiredness, hunger, or transitions, so you can address the root cause before it starts
Practice using a 'regular voice' as a playful game during calm moments, so the skill is already familiar before frustration hits
Celebrate it right away when they switch to a regular voice, so the calmer choice feels worth repeating
Stay calm and consistent - if whining sometimes gets a faster yes than asking normally, it quietly teaches that escalating works
Keep your own reaction steady - a big sigh or a snapped 'stop whining' becomes fuel, since your reaction is often what a spiraling whine is chasing

strategies.name: Name It and Pause
strategies.why_it_works: Narrating what you hear makes your child aware of their communication choice without shaming them, and a strategic pause gives them room to reset instead of reacting to your frustration.
script: I hear your whining. Can you hear it too?
Tell me again in your regular voice - I want to understand what you need.
Take your time. I'm listening.
There it is - thank you for using your regular voice.
strategies.mantra: Their whine is a communication style, not an attack on me. I can stay calm and wait it out.

strategies.name: Ride Out the Repeat
strategies.why_it_works: Removing your attention from the whining behavior, while staying warm and present, lets a spiral run its course without the fuel of a bigger reaction - most kids de-escalate faster once the loop stops getting a rise out of you.
script: I can tell you still need to whine. Let me know when you're done.
I'm here when you're ready to use your regular voice.
I'm not changing my answer, and I'm not going anywhere either.
I believe you can use your regular voice when you're ready.
Thank you for using your regular voice. That was hard work, and I know it.
strategies.mantra: I don't have to fix this whine or win it. I just have to stay steady until it passes.

strategies.name: Check the Tank First
strategies.why_it_works: Whining that won't quit even after a clear answer is often less about the request and more about an empty tank - tiredness or hunger make everything feel harder and voices whinier.
script: I hear a LOT of whining right now. I wonder if your body is tired or hungry.
Tired feelings can make everything feel harder, even little things.
Let's get you a snack and a quiet minute before we talk more.
I'm here to help once your body feels a bit more like itself.
strategies.mantra: A spiraling whine is sometimes a tired body asking for help, not a battle to win.

parenting_scripts.title: Public Meltdown: When Feelings Flood
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child dissolves into a full flood of tears, bolting, or shutting down in a public or social setting - a party, a family gathering, a crowded place - overwhelmed by big feelings
prevention_tips: Pre-agree the plan in a calm moment: tell your child that when feelings get huge, you stay close and never send them away. Most kids quietly welcome hearing this before it's tested
Before any event with a spotlight moment - a birthday song, an award, a big cheer - give advance notice and offer a choice about how much of it they're in for
Watch for buildup before a public outing - hunger, heat, crowd noise - which all raise the odds of a flood
Know your quiet exit route in any public space you're heading into, so you're not searching for one mid-flood
Offer a buffer option ahead of time, like sitting on your lap or watching from the side, instead of assuming they want to be front and center

strategies.name: Go Quiet, Stay Close
strategies.why_it_works: At the peak of a flood, fewer words and less direct eye contact help - a hard, steady gaze can read as threat in a high-alarm state. Staying close and calm without trying to talk them down proves the thing they fear most wrong: their feelings didn't overwhelm you.
script: I'm here. I'm not going anywhere.
You don't have to do anything right now.
Take whatever time you need.
I'll give you a little space - I'm right here, not far.
Here I am. I never went far.
strategies.mantra: Staying calm and close through the peak proves I can hold this. That matters more than any words.

strategies.name: Shrink the Spotlight
strategies.why_it_works: Even warm, positive attention can overwhelm a child having a big-feelings moment. Reading the flinch as normal, not rude or ungrateful, and offering a smaller version of the moment helps them stay regulated without missing out entirely.
script: All those eyes at once is a lot, huh.
You're not being rude - it just feels like too much right now.
Want to watch from my lap, or step to the side with me for a minute?
You don't have to love being the center of attention. We can always do it small.
strategies.mantra: This isn't ingratitude. It's a nervous system that needed a smaller version of the moment.

strategies.name: Repair Sideways, Later
strategies.why_it_works: A face-to-face 'let's talk about what happened' can reopen the shame of a big public moment. Revisiting sideways - hands busy, no eye contact, or planning ahead instead of relitigating - rebuilds the memory without restaging it.
script: That party was a lot today, huh.
Want to invent a secret signal for next time feelings get big? You pick it, I'll follow it.
That was a hard one. We're okay.
We can always do the next one your size.
strategies.mantra: Revisiting sideways, not face-to-face, is what actually helps this child feel safe again.

parenting_scripts.title: The Death Question, Out of Nowhere
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child suddenly asks about death or dying, often at bedtime or in the car, catching you off guard
prevention_tips: Decide your honest, plain-language answer before you need it - 'died' means the body stopped working and won't start again - so you're not improvising in the moment
Treat questions about death like any other big curiosity, the same drive that asks why the sky goes dark, not a topic to steer away from
Avoid soft stand-ins like 'lost', 'sleeping', or 'gone away' even in casual conversation, so those ordinary words stay safe and don't get tied to permanent loss later
Remember most of a child's fear comes from not understanding, not from the facts themselves - a clear, honest answer is calmer than the guess they'd make on their own

This script is for the ordinary out-of-nowhere question. If your child's fear of death becomes intense or doesn't ease over several weeks, or they talk about not wanting to be here, check in with your pediatrician or a child therapist

strategies.name: Answer It Plainly
strategies.why_it_works: A concrete, literal definition gives a child something solid to reason from, where a dreamy or vague one leaves them guessing something scarier. Direct language, paired with your closeness, is what lets them exhale.
script: That's a really good question. Can I tell you the true answer?
When someone dies, their body completely stops working - no breathing, no heartbeat - and it won't start again.
It's really sad, and it's okay to have big feelings about it.
I'm right here with you.
strategies.mantra: Plain and honest, paired with closeness, is what actually settles this - not a perfect sentence.

strategies.name: The Scary Follow-Up
strategies.why_it_works: A flat 'never' is a promise a child eventually catches as untrue, which costs your trustworthiness. An honest answer paired with an immediate, present-tense reassurance settles the fear without the risk of a broken promise.
script: Here's the true answer: everybody dies someday, way far in the future.
I'm healthy, I take good care of myself, and I plan to be here for a very, very long time.
You are safe. I am right here tonight.
Your only job right now is being a kid.
strategies.mantra: Honest and warm beats a perfect promise. The truth, held closely, is what they can trust.

strategies.name: Keep the Door Open
strategies.why_it_works: This is the first of many talks, not the whole job. Kids remember whether their questions were welcomed far longer than they remember the exact words - ending every talk with a real invitation to come back is what makes the next question easier to ask.
script: That's such a good question. You can ask me anything, anytime.
I don't know everything about it, and that's okay - I'll always tell you the truth.
If you think of more questions tomorrow, or next week, I'm right here.
It's okay to feel sad, and it's also okay to go back to playing. Both are fine.
strategies.mantra: One honest, open conversation is a success, even if it wasn't perfectly worded.

parenting_scripts.title: The Phone Handover Battle
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child refuses to hand over the tablet or phone when it's time - clutching it, running off, or negotiating for 'just one more minute' long after the timer is done
prevention_tips: Give every screen a home - a basket or shelf where it lives when it's not in use - so 'time to put it away' is a routine, not a daily negotiation
Use a scheduled-unavailability setting so 'off' lives inside the device itself, instead of being something you have to enforce by hand every time
Close every session the same way - a stand-up, a stretch, 'tell me the best part' - so stopping has a familiar ritual instead of feeling like a cliff
Model it yourself: tuck your own phone into the same basket at the same time, so the rule is something everyone follows, not just a kid rule
If you're about to change the rules because the current setup isn't working, decide the new plan calmly in advance rather than announcing it mid-battle

strategies.name: Warn, Then Close the Ritual
strategies.why_it_works: A session that ends the same way every time - a stand-up, a stretch, naming the best part - turns stopping into a familiar ritual instead of a cliff edge, which makes the actual handover far less of a fight.
script: One more song, then we're done for now.
Big stretch - shake it all out!
Tell me the best part you just watched.
Now it's time for the tablet to go in its basket.
strategies.mantra: A predictable ending is what makes the handover easy, not a bigger warning voice.

strategies.name: Hold the Line, Calmly
strategies.why_it_works: Delivering the handover as a decision you've already made, not a request for buy-in, closes the door on negotiation. Pushback is a sign the limit landed, not that you got it wrong.
script: I know that's a change you didn't want. The tablet goes in the basket now.
You're allowed to be upset about this. I'm not mad at you, and this isn't a punishment.
The basket is where it sleeps - that's true for my phone too.
I'm not asking you to agree. I'm just letting you know what's happening.
I'll help you with the hard part - here, let's do it together.
strategies.mantra: Pushback means the limit landed, not that I got it wrong. I don't need their agreement to hold it.

strategies.name: Let the Device Be the Rule
strategies.why_it_works: A firm, scheduled 'off' built into the device itself is a decision you make once instead of re-litigating every day, and it means the limit comes from the system, not from you personally, which takes some heat out of the handover.
script: It's not me being mean - the tablet's set to go to sleep now, same as every day.
See? It's already locking up for the night. That's not a surprise, that's just how it works.
I'll get a little note if you want a new app, and I always think about it before I say yes.
The settings code stays with the grown-ups, like the medicine-cabinet key. That's just how our house works.
strategies.mantra: A rule the device holds is a rule I don't have to fight for every single time.

parenting_scripts.title: Caught With a Friend's Toy in Their Pocket
parenting_scripts.scenario: You discover your child has pocketed a small toy from a friend's house or a playdate, without asking
prevention_tips: Before playdates, name the rule in advance: things at a friend's house stay at the friend's house, and if something's really loved, you can ask about getting one
Watch for patterns - does this tend to happen after visiting a specific friend, or around toys that feel special or admired? Patterns point to the real driver
Model naming your own wants for things you can't have, out loud, so your child hears the words instead of just feeling the impulse
Keep your own reaction calm and curious rather than alarmed - a big reaction to a small pocketed toy can make hiding feel safer than telling next time
Praise honesty warmly whenever it shows up, even about small things, so telling the truth stays the easier choice

strategies.name: Name It Without Shame
strategies.why_it_works: Calmly stating the fact and labeling the behavior, without accusation or a lecture about trust, keeps your child from having to defend a lie on top of the original slip. Understanding what drove it matters more than treating every incident the same.
script: I found this toy in your pocket. I think this belongs to Maya.
You really liked playing with this at Maya's house.
When we take something that belongs to someone else without asking, that's called stealing.
We need to return this to Maya. How do you think we should do that?
strategies.mantra: This is about a want they didn't know how to voice, not proof my child is dishonest.

strategies.name: Redirect the Want Into Words
strategies.why_it_works: Giving your child the exact words for the wish underneath the action teaches them a workable alternative, instead of just naming what not to do.
script: It's normal to want something you really like.
Next time, you can tell me 'I really want one of these' instead of putting it in your pocket.
Sometimes I'll say yes to getting something similar, sometimes no - but asking is always the right move.
I'm proud of you for telling me the truth now.
strategies.mantra: Every 'you can tell me instead' is a tool they'll actually have next time.

strategies.name: Make It Right, Together
strategies.why_it_works: Involving your child in the actual return builds the repair skill directly, and doing it together, rather than as a solo punishment, keeps the lesson about honesty and repair, not about shame.
script: Let's go give this back to Maya together.
You can say, 'I took this without asking. Sorry - here it is back.'
Taking things without permission can hurt a friendship, even by accident.
That took courage. I'm glad you made it right.
strategies.mantra: Repair done together teaches more than punishment done alone.

parenting_scripts.title: Backtalk With an Audience
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child sasses, refuses, or talks back defiantly in front of other people - other parents, family, a checkout line - and you feel the stares
prevention_tips: Before a known-hard public moment, prime it in advance: 'In a few minutes it's time to go. Your body might yell NO - that's allowed. We'll go anyway.'
Decide ahead of time that the nearest stranger is rooting for you, not scoring you - it's easier to remember before you're in the moment than during it
Treat public moments as get-through-it-safely; save the actual teaching for later, in private, once everyone's calm
Practice a big-feeling redo in calm, playful moments at home, so the skill is available mid-standoff, not just discussed after
Notice your own urge to react harder because people are watching - that urge is about the audience, not about what your child actually needs

strategies.name: Slow Down, Get Curious
strategies.why_it_works: A flat refusal is usually a grab for control, not a genuine debate, so out-arguing it just hands your child something to push against. Reflecting it back with real curiosity removes the wall to push on.
script: You really don't want to. Tell me the worst part.
You wish this didn't have to happen right now. I get it.
That part's still happening. You pick - do we walk to the car, or do I carry you like a sack of potatoes?
That was a big feeling, and it came out unkind. Try it again - I'm listening.
strategies.mantra: I don't have to win this. I only have to hold it - the audience doesn't get a vote.

strategies.name: Answer the Audience in Your Head
strategies.why_it_works: An audience cranks up a parent's fear of being judged, which pushes toward a harsher, faster reaction than the same moment would get at home. Naming that pull silently is what frees you to answer your child instead of the onlookers.
script: I'm not on trial here. My kid needs me, not a show for the aisle.
You wish we could stay. It's SO hard to stop having fun.
This part's decided. You pick how we get there - hop like a frog, or ride on my shoulders?
We'll talk more about it once we're in the car.
strategies.mantra: The strangers leave. The pattern I set with my child is what stays.

strategies.name: Save the Lesson for Later
strategies.why_it_works: Treating the public moment as get-through-it-safely, and moving the actual teaching to a calm, private moment afterward, means neither of you is trying to learn or teach while flooded and watched.
script: Let's just get through this bit - we can talk more once we're home.
I'm not going to fix this here. I'm just going to keep us moving.
Earlier was a hard moment. Want to try that again, just the words this time?
You're allowed to be upset in front of people. I'm not embarrassed by you.
strategies.mantra: Teaching happens later, in private. Right now my only job is getting us through safely.

parenting_scripts.title: When the Big Sibling Hits or Squeezes the Baby
parenting_scripts.scenario: Your older child hits, squeezes too hard, or lashes out at the new baby - sometimes affection turned rough, sometimes clear frustration
prevention_tips: Sort belongings visibly ahead of time - protected treasures up high, shared toys in a basket both kids can reach - so there's less to guard in the moment
Give your older child words for 'no' and 'mine' so their hands don't have to do the talking when the baby gets close to something they care about
Say out loud, more than once, that your love for them stays whole - a new baby doesn't split it
If this keeps happening the same way, treat it as a skill gap rather than defiance, and plan your own response in advance instead of reacting fresh each time
Stay within arm's reach whenever your older child is near the baby during this stretch, so you can block before contact instead of after

strategies.name: Block First, Talk Later
strategies.why_it_works: A child mid-lash-out is running on an overwhelmed system, not executing a plan - language barely gets in. Stepping in with your calm body and very few words delivers the one message that matters: I've got this, everyone's safe.
script: Stop. I'm here. No hitting the baby - I'll help you both.
I won't let you hurt him. I'm keeping everyone safe.
I'm right here with you.
We'll talk once everyone's calm.
strategies.mantra: Safety first, feelings second, talking last. I don't need words to keep everyone safe.

strategies.name: Name the Worry Underneath
strategies.why_it_works: Aggression toward a new baby is usually worry about being replaced, not real dislike of the baby. Naming that fear directly, and saying your love stays whole, addresses what's actually driving the behavior.
script: I think it feels wobbly watching the baby get close to your things, and to me.
This baby is lucky - they get you as a big sibling. And my love for you stays all yours. Nobody can take your share.
You can tell me 'mine' or 'not now' with words. I'll help the baby wait.
Sometimes being the little one looks kind of cozy, huh. Want to play baby for five minutes with me?
strategies.mantra: This is worry wearing the costume of aggression. My job is to answer the worry.

strategies.name: Build the Standing Plan
strategies.why_it_works: When the same thing keeps happening despite calm handling each time, it's a missing skill, not a behavior to punish harder. Giving the grab-or-hit urge one standing, practiced outlet, decided together in a calm moment, is what actually starts to change it.
script: When the baby gets close to your things, your body gets a big push to grab or hit. That push is okay - hitting isn't. Let's give the push somewhere to go.
What could your hands do instead - squeeze this pillow tight, or come find me?
I'm going to stay close by when you two are together, so I can help before it gets big.
This keeps happening because something's missing, not because you're being bad. We're figuring it out together.
strategies.mantra: This keeps coming back because a skill is still missing, not because my child is bad. I can keep hunting for the gap.

parenting_scripts.title: Homework Perfectionism Shutdown
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child rips up their worksheet and insists "I can't do it" after a single mistake
prevention_tips: Praise the sticking-with-it, not just the correct answers, so one mistake doesn't feel like the whole grade
Let your child watch you make a small mistake and move on without a big reaction
Practice tolerating "good enough" on low-stakes tasks before it matters, so it isn't new in the moment that counts
Keep a spare copy of any worksheet on hand so one torn page isn't a crisis
Save handwriting or accuracy feedback for a calm moment, never mid-meltdown
Say out loud when something has no real deadline, so the pressure has one less source

strategies.name: Finish It, Don't Fix It
strategies.why_it_works: In the heat of the moment, correcting the mistake only adds pressure. The skill worth building isn't a clean page. It's staying with an imperfect one until it's done.
script: You got one answer wrong, and right now the whole page feels ruined to you.
We're not erasing anything or starting over. We're finishing this exact page.
Your hand on the pencil. I'm right here next to you.
Look at that. Done, mistake and all. It still counts as finished.
strategies.mantra: Finishing beats fixing. The correction can wait for a calmer day.

strategies.name: Ask About Their Rule
strategies.why_it_works: Letting a child explain their own rule, rather than being told it's wrong, lets them run into their own inconsistency out loud, something no amount of reassurance from you would land as well.
script: So walk me through your rule here. What tips a page from fine into ruined?
Is it any mistake at all, or just this one?
Huh, so one wrong answer erases everything else that's right on the page?
You don't have to answer. I just wanted to hear how the rule works.
strategies.mantra: I don't need to win this. Curiosity does the work for me.

strategies.name: Name the Effort, Not the Score
strategies.why_it_works: Reflecting back the persistence instead of the result teaches a child that trying hard counts on its own, so a perfect outcome slowly loses some of its grip as the only thing that matters.
script: You stayed with this for twenty minutes even when it got hard. That's what I noticed.
I'm not checking whether it's right. I'm watching how you keep going.
Getting stuck and staying in your seat anyway. That's the actual skill.
This worksheet won't matter next week. Not giving up on it will.
strategies.mantra: Effort is what I'm coaching for. The score isn't mine to fix.

parenting_scripts.title: Bath Refusal
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child cries, hides, or bolts the moment you announce it's bath time
prevention_tips: Give a warning a few minutes before bath time starts, not out of nowhere
Let your child help pick a bath toy or towel ahead of time
Start running the water only after they're already in the bathroom, not before
Build a short, predictable pre-bath routine, like a song or a timer, that's the same every night
Ask what part of bath time feels bad on a calm day, not mid-refusal
Offer a quick shower or a sponge-off as an alternative some nights

strategies.name: Name the No, Keep the Plan
strategies.why_it_works: Acknowledging the refusal fully before repeating the requirement lowers the fight. A child who feels heard has less to push against, even when the answer doesn't change.
script: You really don't want a bath tonight. I hear you.
It's still happening. Bath time doesn't skip just because you don't want it.
You can walk in on your own two feet, or I'll carry you. Your choice.
I'm not asking if you want a bath. I'm asking how you want to get there.
strategies.mantra: Their no is real. My answer can still stand next to it.

strategies.name: Hand Over the Order
strategies.why_it_works: Offering real choices over the parts that don't matter gives a child a genuine sense of control inside a requirement that isn't actually negotiable.
script: Bath is happening. You get to run the rest of it.
Rubber duck first or bubbles first. You decide.
Do you want to wash your hair at the start or right at the end?
You're in charge of the order. I'm just in charge of making sure it happens.
strategies.mantra: The bath isn't optional. Almost everything about it can be.

strategies.name: Get Curious, Not Convincing
strategies.why_it_works: Many bath refusals trace back to a specific sensory or fear trigger, like water on the face or the sound of the drain. Naming that plainly gets further than trying to reassure it away.
script: Something about bath time feels bad to you, and I'm not going to argue you out of it.
Is it the water on your face, or something else?
I'll keep the water out of your eyes tonight. Let's try that first.
You don't have to enjoy this part. I just need you to let me help.
strategies.mantra: There's usually a real reason under the refusal. My job is to find it, not out-argue it.

parenting_scripts.title: Teeth Brushing Fight
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child clamps their mouth shut, twists away, or runs from the toothbrush every night
prevention_tips: Brush at the same point in the routine every night so it's never a surprise
Let your child hold the toothbrush and go first before you take a turn
Try a softer brush or a different toothpaste flavor if the sensation seems to be the real problem
Keep brushing short and matter-of-fact. Skip the lecture about cavities
Take turns counting teeth together so it's a shared job, not something done to them
Brush your own teeth next to them without asking anything of them at all

strategies.name: Name It Plainly, Hold the Line
strategies.why_it_works: Naming exactly what's uncomfortable about brushing, without trying to talk them out of the feeling, lowers resistance more than explaining why teeth need brushing ever does.
script: The toothbrush bugs you. The bristles, the taste, the whole feeling of it. I know.
It's happening anyway. Teeth need this every single night.
Do you want to hold it, or should I?
Two minutes and it's done. Then we're free.
strategies.mantra: Understanding the discomfort and still following through aren't opposites.

strategies.name: Hand Over One Real Piece
strategies.why_it_works: Giving a small, genuine piece of control, like who holds the brush or which teeth go first, turns a task done to a child into one done with them, which lowers the urge to fight it.
script: You pick. Top teeth first or bottom teeth first?
You hold it and go first. I'll finish up after.
Want to count how many teeth we get to today?
You're doing the hard part. I'm just helping at the end.
strategies.mantra: A little real control now buys a lot less fighting later.

strategies.name: Make It Silly
strategies.why_it_works: Playfulness shifts a child out of a defensive, dug-in state. A shared laugh often opens a mouth that no amount of insisting could.
script: I bet there's a piece of broccoli hiding way back there. Let's go hunt for it.
Open wide. I need to check if any sugar bugs moved in today.
Should we brush like a lion or a dinosaur tonight?
Found one! Two more swipes and the sugar bugs are all gone.
strategies.mantra: Silly gets further than serious most nights. I can let this be easy.

parenting_scripts.title: Getting Dressed Standoff
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child refuses every outfit, strips back off what you put on, or plants themselves half-dressed and won't move
prevention_tips: Lay out two acceptable outfit choices together the night before
Build a real time buffer into the morning so dressing isn't racing the clock
Let your child dress in whatever order they want, even if it's backward
Cut out scratchy tags or switch to softer fabrics if texture seems to be the trigger
Settle your own urgency first. A rushed voice tends to make the standoff worse, not faster
Put the hardest dressing step earliest in the routine, before screens or breakfast compete for attention

strategies.name: Choose How, Not Whether
strategies.why_it_works: Offering a real choice about the order or manner of dressing, never about whether it happens, gives them a small, genuine say without reopening the one thing that isn't up for negotiation.
script: You don't have to want this. Getting dressed is happening either way.
You choose which shirt. The striped one or the plain one.
Want to get dressed on the bed, or race me to the rug?
Socks or shirt first. You're driving that part.
strategies.mantra: The whether is mine to hold. Almost everything else is theirs to decide.

strategies.name: Settle Your Body First
