strategies.why_it_works: Children pick up on a parent's rush and often push back harder against it. Slowing your own voice and movement removes some of the fuel the standoff is running on.
script: I'm going to slow down for a second, even though we're behind.
I'm not going to chase you around the room for this shirt.
I'll wait right here until you're ready to try again.
We have a few minutes. Let's use them instead of losing them.
strategies.mantra: My calm isn't a reward for their cooperation. It comes first, not after.

strategies.name: Gentle Follow-Through
strategies.why_it_works: When a stall goes past a fair amount of waiting, finishing the task with your child instead of to them keeps the boundary standing without turning it into a bigger battle.
script: You've had a few minutes to choose, and that's okay. I'll help now.
Arm through here, now this side. We're doing it together.
We're not fighting about this. It's just happening now, gently.
There. Done. That was the hard part, and you got through it.
strategies.mantra: Following through calmly is still kind. Firm doesn't have to mean a fight.

parenting_scripts.title: Playground Leaving Refusal
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child sprints back to the climbing structure, goes limp, or melts down as soon as you say it's time to go
prevention_tips: Give a concrete warning, like "one more turn, then we're leaving," instead of a vague one
Walk over and close the distance before giving the leaving instruction. Don't call it across the playground
Build a small leaving ritual, like waving goodbye to the slide, into the good days
Avoid promising a return trip unless it's genuinely certain
Plan arrival time with a buffer so leaving doesn't collide with another deadline
Talk about the fun on the way to the car instead of the fact that it's over

strategies.name: Walk Over Before You Call Out
strategies.why_it_works: An instruction shouted across a playground tends to start a chase. Walking over and speaking at their level before naming the limit keeps the moment from turning into catch-me-if-you-can.
script: I'm coming over to tell you this, not yelling it from the bench.
Playtime is ending now. That part isn't changing.
Want to zoom to the car like a rocket, or walk it slow with me?
I'm staying right beside you either way.
strategies.mantra: Other parents aren't grading this moment. My kid needs me close, not loud.

strategies.name: Validate the Want, Then the Limit
strategies.why_it_works: Naming how much they wanted to keep playing, fully and before anything else, tends to shrink the protest that follows. A child who feels understood has less left to push against.
script: You wish you could stay on that climber all afternoon.
Leaving something this fun is genuinely hard. I'm not surprised you're upset.
And we still have to go right now. Both things are true.
Tell me the best part while we walk, so I don't forget it either.
strategies.mantra: Their disappointment is real. It doesn't mean the boundary is wrong.

strategies.name: Calm Carry, Teach Later
strategies.why_it_works: Once a child has gone limp or is mid-meltdown, explanations stop landing. Picking them up calmly and saving the conversation for afterward keeps everyone safer and ends the standoff faster than more words would.
script: You can't hear me right now, so I'm going to carry you.
You don't have to walk. I've got you.
We'll talk about all of this once we're both calm.
I'm not angry. Big feelings about leaving fun places make total sense.
strategies.mantra: When words stop working, a calm action can still be kind.

parenting_scripts.title: Swear Word Shock
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child drops a swear word or shock word out loud, sometimes in front of other people
prevention_tips: Notice your own reaction to strong language before it happens, so a big flinch doesn't teach the word is powerful
Talk about which words are okay where on a calm day, before the next slip
Give your child a few silly alternative words they're free to use when they want to feel big or shocking
Avoid repeating the word back loudly or asking who taught it to them in the moment
Keep your response short and similar every time so it isn't an exciting reaction worth chasing

strategies.name: Stay Flat, Don't Feed It
strategies.why_it_works: A strong reaction is often exactly what makes a shock word worth repeating. Responding calmly and briefly removes the payoff without shaming the curiosity behind it.
script: Sounds like you found a word that gets a big reaction.
That word doesn't get used here. That's not changing.
You're not in trouble for learning a new word.
Let's find one that does the same job without the trouble.
strategies.mantra: My calm face is the least interesting response I can give this.

strategies.name: Name What It Felt Like
strategies.why_it_works: Acknowledging that the word probably felt exciting or grown-up to say helps a child feel understood rather than caught, which makes them more willing to accept where the line actually is.
script: I bet that word felt big to say, like a grown-up word.
Wanting to feel big and bold is okay. That particular word just isn't how we do it here.
What's a word that could feel just as strong, without the trouble it causes?
There are lots of ways to be loud and bold that don't get you in trouble.
strategies.mantra: The urge behind the word is fine. Only the word itself needs a new home.

strategies.name: Repair in Front of Others
strategies.why_it_works: When the word lands in front of other people, a brief, light acknowledgment protects your child from public embarrassment while staying honest that it wasn't the right moment. The real conversation happens later, in private.
script: That's a word we're still learning about. We'll talk about it at home.
Sorry about that. We're working on it.
Let's go find something else to do right now.
We'll talk more about that word later, just us.
strategies.mantra: The real conversation happens in private, not in front of an audience.

parenting_scripts.title: Refuses to Apologize
parenting_scripts.scenario: Child hurt someone, a sibling or a friend, and goes silent, stiff, or defiant rather than say sorry
prevention_tips: Model your own apologies openly, including to your child, so they see what repair looks like
Avoid demanding "say sorry" in front of an audience. It tends to backfire
Talk about mistakes as things everyone makes, on calm days, not just in the moment
Keep your own reaction calm when they hurt someone, so shame doesn't lock the door before repair can start
Give repair a low-pressure shape beyond the word "sorry," like drawing a picture or checking if the other person is okay

strategies.name: Lower the Shame First
strategies.why_it_works: A stuck apology is rarely missing remorse. It's usually shame locking the moment shut. Making clear that one unkind moment doesn't define them brings the temperature down enough for repair to become possible again.
script: You're not a bad kid. What just happened was unkind. Those are two different things.
You don't have to have the words ready right this second.
We're going to fix this together. You're not doing it alone.
Take a breath with me before we go back over there.
strategies.mantra: Shame blocks repair. My job is to lower it, not add to it.

strategies.name: Model It, Then Let It Stand
strategies.why_it_works: When the words genuinely won't come, saying them yourself on your child's behalf mends things for the person who got hurt and quietly hands your child language they can borrow next time, without forcing a performance.
script: I'm going to say this part for you, since it's stuck right now.
He didn't mean for that to happen. We're going to make it right together.
Let's go check that you're really okay.
Thank you for staying with me through this instead of running off.
strategies.mantra: A repair I model still counts. My child doesn't have to perform the words today.

strategies.name: The Private Debrief, Later
strategies.why_it_works: Correcting a child in front of the person they hurt tends to trigger more shutdown, not learning. A calm, one-on-one conversation once everyone has settled gives them room to actually reflect instead of just defend.
script: Let's go over what happened earlier, just the two of us.
You looked like something was already bothering you before that happened. What was it?
Words can land harder than we plan for them to. How do you want to handle it now?
Next time that feeling shows up, what's something else you could do with it?
strategies.mantra: The real learning happens later, in private, not in front of anyone else.

universal_phrases.title: Big Emotions
universal_phrases.description: Phrases to acknowledge and validate intense feelings
phrases: This feels really big for you right now.
Your feelings make total sense.
Even when you're upset, I love you.
Those are some really powerful feelings.
Big feelings are okay. I'm here for you.

universal_phrases.title: Setting Boundaries
universal_phrases.description: Phrases to maintain limits while acknowledging feelings
phrases: My answer is still [boundary].
I'll keep you safe, even when you don't like it.
This is hard AND it's still happening.
You can be upset AND we're still doing this.
I hear you don't like it, and we still need to do it.

universal_phrases.title: Connection & Support
universal_phrases.description: Phrases to strengthen attachment during difficult moments
phrases: We'll get through this together.
I'm right here for you.
You can handle this, I know it.
You're not alone in this.
Even when it's hard, I'm on your side.

universal_phrases.title: Parent Self-Regulation
universal_phrases.description: Mantras to help parents stay calm
phrases: We're safe. This isn't an emergency.
Big feelings don't mean I'm doing something wrong.
Being consistent is being kind, even when it's tough.
This will pass. These feelings are temporary.
I can stay calm even when my child can't.

universal_phrases.title: Emotional Validation
universal_phrases.description: Phrases to help children feel heard and understood
phrases: That sounds really [hard/frustrating/disappointing].
I can see why you would feel that way.
If I were you, I might feel [emotion] too.
Your feelings are important to me.
It makes sense that you would want [thing they want].

universal_phrases.title: Choices & Autonomy
universal_phrases.description: Phrases to give children control within boundaries
phrases: You get to choose: [option A] or [option B].
What would feel better for your body right now?
How do you want to handle this?
You're in charge of [specific thing within boundary].
What would help you feel more ready for [transition/task]?

emergency_quick_tips.title: Public Meltdowns
emergency_quick_tips.description: Remember: Other people's opinions don't define your parenting. Focus on your child, not the stares.

emergency_quick_tips.title: Safety First
emergency_quick_tips.description: When behavior involves physical safety, act first and process emotions later.

emergency_quick_tips.title: When to Take Breaks
emergency_quick_tips.description: If you feel yourself losing patience, it's okay to say 'I need a minute to calm down' and step away briefly.

emergency_quick_tips.title: When to Seek Help
emergency_quick_tips.description: Seek support if tantrums increase in frequency/intensity, include self-harm, or if you feel overwhelmed consistently.

age_specific_notes.title: Toddlers
age_specific_notes.description: Toddlers have big emotions but small coping skills. Extra patience and simple language work best.

age_specific_notes.title: Preschoolers
age_specific_notes.description: Can understand more complex explanations but still need concrete choices and clear boundaries.

age_specific_notes.title: School Age
age_specific_notes.description: Can participate in problem-solving but may still need help regulating intense emotions.
